title: A serious question about your workflow
author: OGwargreed
selftext: Hey, I'm a newbie practically in AI Gamedev stuff, but before my job as software developer I actually played a bit with Unreal Engine 5, although that was like 6 years ago , but I guess I still know basics of game dev theory. Also, I'm still familiar with Blender tool and all the stuff needed to create a game asset(sculpting, retopology, texture baking, texture painting, rigging...) as that part was something I've been returning back to occasionally while I was developer. Now that I lost my job and no longer stare at screen for 8(or sometimes more) hours a day, my passion for game dev is rekindled, especially when I see what you guys are making here. Tbh I really did quite a lot of search already on all the tools, installed and tried Trellis 2 with ComfyUI and Tripo AI for asset generation, also tryed to make some mods with claude on other games, but I am still kind of overwhelmed with options out there and what to do exactly. If I must narrow it down, I guess I want to use Unreal Engine again with claude and some 3D asset generator to speed up my process, and currently don't know what to start with exactly. It would help knowing some tested workflows from you guys. I see a lot of people using Godot these days. Is it really better alternative for Unreal Engine or is it just the enthusiasm of it's users? Also, any tip at all would help immensely.

comments.author: imlo2
comments.body:
Godot or Unity. I would pick Godot if you want to stay open source/away from potential license and use costs like with Unity. Both have MCP servers available, a few different ones.  
But if you want high-end 3D, then go with Unreal. Godot and Unity can be very good and lighter for a variety of quite sophisticated 3D things too, you just need to build more on top of them.

I would keep it simple and just start with Claude (gives you much more usage than ChatGPT right now).  
Install Claude Code and have it set your MCPs up, and other environment things, and then you can also use it to drive your local things, but set up another ComfyUI instance for it. But it's now trivial to automate model generation, and create a few steps of image generation, potential clean-up, 3D model generation, and so on.   
You can get away with a lot of 3D stuff being early on generated by the models (Claude or Codex) via Blender, or without pre-built DCC tools (they most likely build some Python tools for this.)  
And of course work on the actual coding / setting up things in the game engine.

But the models can help you with the technical things, I think right now it's more important than ever to decide what you want to build, not so much how you do it.

comments.author: SidAkrita
comments.body:
I used Unity and Unreal when I was an game dev intern (got no job, job market is fucked), learned to use Unity and Unreal at school, but used Godot and tried some other engines and frameworks. I make games on my free time now, and I only use Godot.

You won't be able to do certain things with Godot, but I think if you work alone you won't be able to do them with either engine. Unreal might be best for bigger teams, Unity for mobile and VR maybe, but generally Unreal and Unity are the most used because it's what the industry is used mostly, game studios have built tools for a lot of years now and moving to another engine would be really costly.

For solo devs and people that are starting, Godot is a great tool I think. It's super easy to use, light weight, and every file is just plain text, so it makes it easy for AI to work with it. I don't use MCP with Godot, I don't see the point with Opus now.

For the art I don't have much to say, I tried to do some things with meshy and some 2D generative AI, but I only got slop assets. I stick to 2D for now, I use Krita and custom tools built by Opus to help me. For example I defined a "doodle" style for 2D assets, Opus generates basic shapes and then scripts handle the rest directly inside Krita. I think this is how you want to work for assets.

tldr: IMO Unreal is overkill for you, Unity is just trash, Godot is lightweight and super easy to understand for LLMs, or use any other engine or framework you feel best with. Don't use out of the box generated 2D and 3D assets, build your own pipeline around "real" programs (Blender, Krita, Photoshop...) with the help of AI.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
Hmm unity is trash huh?

I’ve been really trying to figure out how much of what Unity does is really necessary, it does seem like a lot of platform if I’m not going to be using a bunch of stuff from it. But as I understand it has a lot of built in lighting and other effects that I don’t know if I want to have to build from scratch. Is that the right way to think about things?

If you were to build a game from godot, how much more time recreating features that already exist in Unity do you think it needs? I guess the trade off is that you then bypass a lot of bloated features that you DON’T need and you ship a cleaner game right?

replies.author: SidAkrita
replies.body:
Saying Unity is trash was a bit of a joke actually, lots of awesome and beautiful games are made with Unity. I'm not a tech artist so I won't be able to talk about lighting, for the bits I know about this Unity is a mess right now, there were 3 renderers, they announced they were merging everything under one big system, but then they fired everyone working on this. I don't know where Unity is right now, but the lighting system was always something difficult when I saw people trying to use it.

I'm not sure Godot's lighting features are better though, there's work being done and for what I tried it just works, some people do great things (check out PVKK, it's a great Godot flagship) but it's certainly limited compared to Unity or Unreal.

To answer your question it all depends on what you are trying to make. I made a small demo for a boomer shooter with Godot some time ago, everything worked fine because I didn't need super realistic features. When I was intern on an Unreal project, lighting was a huge topic and even if Godot wouldn't be able to give the same output, it needed one tech artist, one developer, and multiple artists to make it work.

comments.author: RoyInProgress
comments.body:
Hey!

I’m a newbie myself, but use Godot and very happy with the results so far.

I asked my Chat about the engines and he told me:

“Unity – A versatile engine for both 2D and 3D games. Widely used in professional and indie development, with a huge ecosystem of tools and assets. Powerful but relatively complex.

Unreal Engine – Best known for high-end 3D games, realistic graphics, and advanced visual effects. Extremely powerful, but demanding and often overkill for smaller 2D projects.

Godot – A free, open-source engine particularly well suited for 2D indie games, RPGs, and smaller 3D projects. Lightweight, flexible, and relatively beginner-friendly. Its readable code and text-based project files make it attractive for AI-assisted development.

Popularity: Unity and Unreal dominate the professional industry, while Godot is growing rapidly among indie developers. Godot appears particularly attractive for AI-assisted game development, although reliable adoption statistics are limited.”
